entries.question: Who is the most blessed woman?
entries.summary: Gabriel tells Mary in Luke 1:28 that she is 'blessed among women.' The Song of Deborah (Judg 5:24) calls Jael 'blessed above women' for driving a tent peg through Sisera's skull. Judith 13:18 calls Judith 'blessed above all women on the earth' for decapitating Holofernes. Three texts each elevate a different woman to the superlative of female blessedness.
entries.commentary:
This one looks like a sharper contradiction than it actually is, but it still has teeth. The Greek of Luke 1:28 — eulogemene su en gynaixin — is the same idiomatic 'blessed among women' construction used in the Septuagint of Judges 5:24 for Jael (eulogetheie ek gynaikon) and in the Greek of Judith 13:18 for Judith. The blessing-formula is essentially a Semitic superlative meaning 'most blessed of women.' If you take any one of these texts on its own, that's the natural reading. Taken together, three different women each occupy the top of that scale.

The usual harmonization runs in two directions. The first, found in Joseph Fitzmyer's Anchor Bible Luke commentary, is that 'blessed among women' is not a strict ranking but a Semitic intensifier — each woman is blessed in her own context for her own act, and the superlative is rhetorical rather than absolute. That's a reasonable linguistic point. The second move, common in Catholic Mariological literature, is to say Luke 1:28 is the eschatological climax that 'completes' the earlier blessings — Mary is the true superlative, and Jael and Judith were just typological foreshadowings. That's a theological reading that requires reading Luke as deliberately overwriting Judges and Judith.

The more interesting critical observation is the literary one. Brittany Wilson and others have noted that Luke seems to deliberately echo Judith's blessing-formula when he frames Mary's. The author of Luke knows the Septuagint and probably knows Judith — Judith was widely circulated in Greek-speaking Jewish circles by the first century. If Luke is consciously cross-referencing, then he's appropriating an existing 'most blessed woman' formula and applying it to Mary, which is exactly what an evangelist promoting the Christ-mother would do. Whether that counts as 'contradiction' depends on whether you read the formula as a ranking or a rhetorical pattern.

The parsimonious reading is that 'blessed among women' is a Semitic idiom for an exceptionally honored woman, and that three different biblical texts apply it to three different women without coordinating their claims. Calling that a hard logical contradiction overstates the case. Calling it a tension that requires harmonization — yes, it's that. The apologist who insists Mary is uniquely 'most blessed' has to demote the Judges and Judith uses to mere foreshadowing, which is a theological choice the texts themselves don't authorize.

commentary_out.commentary:
On its face this looks like a contest of superlatives, but the linguistic spine of all three texts is a single Semitic idiom, and that is where the analysis must begin. The Greek of Luke 1:28 — εὐλογημένη σὺ ἐν γυναιξίν (eulogēmenē su en gynaixin), 'blessed are you among women' — reproduces almost verbatim the Septuagint construction applied to Jael in Judges 5:24 (εὐλογηθείη ἐκ γυναικῶν, eulogētheiē ek gynaikōn) and the formula applied to Judith in the Greek of Judith 13:18 (εὐλογητὴ σὺ … παρὰ πάσας τὰς γυναῖκας τὰς ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς). The prepositional phrase 'among/above women' functions as a periphrastic superlative in Hebrew and its Greek calque: it singles out a woman as supremely honored relative to her sex, exactly as 'fairest among women' works in Song of Songs 1:8. So the question 'who is the MOST blessed woman?' is partly an artifact of reading three independent uses of one stock blessing-formula as if they were coordinated entries on a single ranked list.

The textual data also bear on the Lukan side. The longer reading of Luke 1:28 that adds 'blessed are you among women' (εὐλογημένη σὺ ἐν γυναιξίν) is absent from the earliest and best witnesses (P⁴, ℵ, B, L, W) and is widely judged a scribal harmonization imported from Elizabeth's later acclamation in Luke 1:42, where the phrase is textually secure. Metzger's Textual Commentary treats it as an interpolation; the NA28 brackets it accordingly. The 'contradiction' at 1:28 is therefore in part a product of the Textus Receptus and the KJV the question quotes. The substantive comparison stands at Luke 1:42, where Elizabeth's words to Mary echo the same idiom that crowned Jael and Judith.

Two harmonizing strategies deserve a fair hearing. The first, articulated by Joseph Fitzmyer in the Anchor Bible Luke, is linguistic: the formula is an intensifier, not an absolute ranking, so each woman is supremely blessed within the rhetorical frame of her own narrative without any of them displacing the others. This is the strongest move and it is largely correct as grammar. The second, common in Mariological literature, reads Luke as the eschatological climax that fulfills and supersedes the earlier blessings, making Jael and Judith typological foreshadowings of Mary. That is a coherent theological construal, but it requires reading Luke as deliberately overwriting Judges and Judith — a claim the text asserts nowhere and which the formula's idiomatic character does not require.

The more illuminating critical observation is literary and intertextual. Brittany Wilson and others have argued that Luke consciously evokes the Jael and Judith blessings precisely to invert them: where Jael and Judith are blessed for acts of decapitating, peg-driving violence against enemy commanders, Mary is blessed as the bearer of the prince of peace. Judith circulated widely in Greek-speaking Jewish circles by the first century, and Luke's demonstrable command of the LXX makes literary dependence plausible. If so, Luke is not contradicting the earlier texts but appropriating their honorific pattern and redirecting it — an act of allusion, not arithmetic competition.

Weighing this, the entry is best classified as overstated rather than as a hard logical contradiction. A genuine contradiction would require that the texts assert mutually exclusive propositions about the same referent; instead they apply a conventional superlative idiom to three different women in three different settings, none claiming the others are not blessed. The seam that remains is real but modest: the canon does deploy 'most blessed of women' more than once, and a flat-footed literal reading produces an apparent rivalry that the idiom itself dissolves. The apologist who insists on Mary's unique supremacy must demote the Jael and Judith uses to mere foreshadowing — a theological preference, not a textual datum — but the skeptic who calls this a square contradiction must ignore both the idiom and the textual weakness of Luke 1:28. Verdict: overstated; a Semitic superlative idiom applied to three women, compounded by a secondary scribal reading at Luke 1:28.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: 'Blessed among/above women' is a periphrastic Semitic superlative idiom, not a coordinated ranking; it honors each woman within her own narrative frame without excluding the others. The apparent rivalry at Luke 1:28 is further weakened by the verse's secondary textual status (the phrase is a scribal harmonization from Luke 1:42, absent in P4, Aleph, B, L, W).

entries.question: Were the Philistines subdued all the days of Samuel?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 7:13 says 'the Philistines were subdued, and they came no more into the coast of Israel: and the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel.' 1 Samuel 13:5-10 shows the Philistines invading with massive force during Saul's reign while Samuel is still alive and active. The 'subdued all the days of Samuel' summary in chapter 7 is contradicted by the very next major narrative episode.
entries.commentary:
1 Samuel 7:13 is a Deuteronomistic summary statement closing out the Samuel-at-Mizpah episode: the Philistines are subdued, they don't come into Israelite territory anymore, and Yahweh's hand is against them 'all the days of Samuel.' This is a sweeping claim about the duration of Samuel's lifetime. Just six chapters later in 1 Samuel 13, the Philistines are mustering thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and an army 'as the sand which is on the sea shore in multitude' against Israel — and Samuel is still alive and actively prophetic in the same chapter (1 Sam 13:8-15). The Philistines don't get permanently subdued during Samuel's lifetime; they remain Israel's principal military adversary right through Saul's reign and into David's.

The usual harmonization, found in Tsumura's NICOT commentary and earlier in Keil, distinguishes between 'subdued' (defeated in the immediate Mizpah victory) and 'never invaded again' — claiming the verse only means the Philistines didn't conduct major invasions for some indefinite period after Mizpah, not that they were permanently neutralized for Samuel's entire life. That's a defensible attempt, but the verse explicitly says 'all the days of Samuel' (kol yemei shemuel), and the next major military narrative in the same book has the Philistines back on offensive operations while Samuel is alive.

The critical reading, from McCarter's Anchor Bible 1 Samuel and Antony Campbell's work on the Deuteronomistic History, is that 1 Samuel 7:13 is a redactional summary characteristic of the Deuteronomistic editor's style — a closing-formula declaration that idealizes Samuel's judgeship the way similar summaries idealize earlier judges (Judges 3:11, 'the land had rest forty years'). These are theological closures, not historical chronicles. The actual narrative material in chapters 9-15 doesn't conform to the summary statement because the Deuteronomistic editor stitched together pre-existing narrative units (the rise of Saul, the Philistine wars) without harmonizing them against his own closing formulas.

The apologist 'limited subduing' reading requires you to read 'all the days of Samuel' as 'for some unspecified period during Samuel's days,' which strips the temporal claim of its force. The parsimonious reading is that the Deuteronomistic editor's idealized summary in 7:13 doesn't match the subsequent narrative material in the same book, and the contradiction is a redactional artifact rather than a historical claim about how long the Philistines actually stayed quiet.

commentary_out.commentary:
1 Samuel 7:13 closes the Mizpah deliverance with a sweeping summary: "So the Philistines were subdued (*wayyikkanʿu*), and they came no more into the territory of Israel; and the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel." The phrase *kol yemei shemuʾel*, "all the days of Samuel," frames the claim as covering Samuel's entire lifetime. Yet six chapters later, in 1 Samuel 13:5, the Philistines muster against Israel "thirty thousand chariots and six thousand horsemen and troops like the sand on the seashore," encamp at Michmash, and dominate Israel so thoroughly that the Israelites hide in caves (13:6) and possess no smiths to make weapons (13:19-22). Samuel is unmistakably still alive and active in the same chapter, arriving at Gilgal to rebuke Saul (13:8-15); he does not die until 1 Samuel 25:1. The Philistines remain Israel's principal adversary through Saul's whole reign and into David's. The summary statement and the subsequent narrative do not cohere.

The standard harmonization, defended in Tsumura's NICOT and earlier in Keil & Delitzsch, distinguishes two senses of the verse. "Subdued" describes the immediate, decisive defeat at Mizpah; "came no more into the territory of Israel" is read as referring to a bounded period of Philistine quiescence after that victory, not permanent neutralization; and "the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel" is taken as a general statement of divine disposition rather than a claim of unbroken Israelite military supremacy. On this reading, the Philistines could still wage war (chapter 13) while Yahweh's hand remained fundamentally against them across Samuel's career. This is the strongest form of the apologetic, and it is not absurd: Hebrew narrative summaries do at times state tendencies rather than exceptionless facts.

The difficulty is the explicit temporal totality of the clause. "They came no more into the territory of Israel... all the days of Samuel" is not naturally read as "for a while," and chapter 13 has the Philistines doing precisely what 7:13 says they would not do — penetrating deep into Israelite territory — while Samuel lives. The apologetic reading must convert "all the days of Samuel" into "during some unspecified stretch of Samuel's days," which drains the temporal claim of its force.

The critical reading, following McCarter's Anchor Bible *1 Samuel* and Antony Campbell's form-critical work on the Deuteronomistic History, identifies 7:13 as a redactional closing formula characteristic of the Deuteronomistic editor. It functions exactly like the idealizing judge-summaries in Judges — "and the land had rest forty years" (Judg 3:11; 5:31; 8:28) — which round off a deliverance episode with a theological declaration of peace under a divinely raised leader. Such formulas express the editor's schema of judgeship, not a chronicle. The Mizpah narrative itself is framed by the Ebenezer stone (7:12), a memorial of victory, and the summary completes that literary frame. Martin Noth's classic analysis explains why the friction exists: the Deuteronomist stitched together pre-existing narrative blocks — the Samuel traditions, the rise of Saul, the Philistine wars — and laid his own summarizing formulas over them without harmonizing the seams. The result is that 7:13 idealizes Samuel's judgeship as a period of Philistine subjugation while the source material in chapters 9-15 portrays continuing Philistine dominance.

The "limited subduing" harmonization can be made to work only by softening "all the days of Samuel" into a vague interval, which the Hebrew resists. The more economical explanation is that 7:13 is a Deuteronomistic theological closure that the editor did not reconcile against the narrative he subsequently included. Verdict: genuine internal tension, best explained as a redactional summary formula at odds with the source narrative.

entries.question: Why was Saul rejected as king?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 13:9-14 has Samuel telling Saul his dynasty is ended because Saul offered the burnt offering himself instead of waiting. 1 Samuel 15:11, 23 has Yahweh declaring he regrets making Saul king because Saul spared Agag and the best Amalekite livestock instead of completing the genocide. The two chapters give two different rejection events with two different stated causes.
entries.commentary:
This is a textbook duplication problem in the books of Samuel. Saul gets rejected twice — once in 1 Samuel 13 for premature sacrifice at Gilgal, and once in 1 Samuel 15 for incomplete extermination of the Amalekites. Each rejection narrative is structurally complete: a divine command, a failure, a prophetic confrontation, and a declaration that Yahweh has rejected Saul as king. Critical scholarship — going back to Wellhausen and forward through McCarter, Klein, and Antony Campbell — has read these as parallel rejection traditions preserved side by side, not as a sequential narrative of progressive divine displeasure.

The apologist harmonization, found in Tsumura's NICOT and in most evangelical Samuel commentaries, treats the two rejections as sequential: in chapter 13 Saul's dynasty is rejected (his sons won't inherit the kingship), and in chapter 15 Saul himself is rejected (Yahweh tears the kingdom from him personally). That distinction works as a reading move, but it requires you to take very similar prophetic-rejection language in both chapters and assign it different referents based on what the later narrative requires. In 1 Samuel 13:14 Samuel says 'thy kingdom shall not continue' (lo' taqum mamlakhtekha) — a dynastic claim. In 1 Samuel 15:23 Samuel says 'he hath also rejected thee from being king' (vayyim'asakha mi-melekh) — a personal claim. The two rejections do differ on this point, and the apologetic reading captures that distinction.

But the larger problem is that both chapters are structured as the moment of decisive divine repudiation. The narrative in 1 Samuel 15:11 has Yahweh saying 'It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king' — and that's framed as the actual turning point, with no reference back to chapter 13 as an earlier rejection. Samuel and Saul never see each other again after chapter 15 (per 15:35), and David's anointing happens immediately in chapter 16 as the direct consequence of the chapter 15 rejection. The narrative treats chapter 15 as the cause of the dynastic change, not chapter 13.

McCarter's Anchor Bible 1 Samuel treats this as a duplication produced by the joining of independent source traditions about Saul's downfall. Antony Campbell's FOTL volume and Klein's WBC see the same pattern. There were probably multiple traditions in early Israel about why the house of Saul failed, and the redactor included both prominent ones — the sacrifice tradition and the Amalek tradition — without forcing them into a single chronology of sin. The harmonizer's 'dynasty rejected first, person rejected second' reading is grammatically possible, but it's a smoothing move imposed on what looks like a redactional doublet. The parsimonious reading is that the canon preserves two separate rejection traditions, and the question 'why was Saul rejected?' depends on which tradition you read.

commentary_out.commentary:
Saul is rejected as king twice in 1 Samuel, in two structurally complete and independently motivated episodes. In 1 Samuel 13:8-14, Saul, waiting at Gilgal for Samuel and watching his army desert, offers the burnt offering himself; Samuel arrives, condemns the act, and announces that Saul's kingship will not endure. In 1 Samuel 15, Saul wins the Amalekite war but spares King Agag and the best livestock in violation of the *ḥerem* command; Yahweh declares regret at having made Saul king, and Samuel pronounces him rejected. Each episode follows the same form — divine command, failure, prophetic confrontation, declaration of rejection — and each reads as the decisive moment of repudiation. Critical scholarship from Wellhausen onward, and through McCarter, Klein, and Antony Campbell, treats these as parallel rejection traditions set side by side, not as two stages of a single escalating process.

The apologetic harmonization, defended in Tsumura's NICOT and most evangelical Samuel commentaries, reads the two as sequential and distinct in scope: chapter 13 rejects Saul's *dynasty* (his line will not inherit the throne), while chapter 15 rejects Saul *personally* (Yahweh tears the kingship from Saul himself). The lexical data give this reading real purchase. In 13:14 Samuel says *loʾ taqum mamlakhtekha*, "your kingdom will not stand/continue" — a statement about the endurance of Saul's reign or line. In 15:23 Samuel says *wayyimʾasakha mi-melekh*, "he has rejected you from being king" — a statement about Saul's own status. The two declarations are not verbally identical, and the harmonist is right that they can be distinguished as dynastic versus personal repudiation. This is the strongest form of the reconciling case.

The difficulty is that the narrative does not treat chapter 13 as a prior, lesser rejection that chapter 15 completes. 1 Samuel 15:11 frames Yahweh's regret — "It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king" — as the turning point, with no backward reference to a rejection already pronounced in chapter 13. After chapter 15 Samuel and Saul never meet again (15:35), and the consequence flows directly: in chapter 16 Samuel anoints David as the replacement, explicitly because Yahweh has rejected Saul (16:1). The dynastic transfer is narratively grounded in chapter 15, not chapter 13. If chapter 13 had already ended Saul's dynasty, chapter 15's rejection and the immediate move to anoint David would be redundant rather than climactic. There is also a chronological strain: 1 Samuel 13:1 opens with a regnal formula and 13:8-14 places the first rejection at the very start of Saul's reign, yet Saul continues to rule and to be treated as legitimately king for years afterward, which fits awkwardly with a definitive dynastic termination in his first regnal acts.

McCarter's Anchor Bible *1 Samuel* reads the doublet as the product of joining independent traditions about why the house of Saul failed; Campbell's FOTL volume and Klein's WBC concur, and Wellhausen's *Prolegomena* gave the classic source-critical statement that early Israel preserved more than one explanation of Saul's downfall — a cultic-offense tradition and an Amalekite-*ḥerem* tradition — which the editor incorporated without collapsing into a single sequence of escalating guilt. The harmonist's dynasty-then-person scheme is grammatically available and captures a genuine difference in the two declarations, but it imposes a smoothing logic on what bears the marks of a redactional doublet: two complete rejection scenes, each presented as decisive, neither cross-referencing the other. Verdict: genuine doublet — the canon preserves two distinct rejection traditions, and the harmonizing sequence, while possible, is read into rather than out of the text.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The dynastic-vs-personal reading has lexical support (13:14 'your kingdom will not stand' vs. 15:23 'rejected you from being king') and can sequence the two episodes; but the narrative frames chapter 15 as the decisive turning point with no back-reference to chapter 13, and the scenes show the form of an unreconciled source doublet, so the resolution remains contested.

entries.question: How many sons did Jesse have?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 16:10-11 and 17:12 give Jesse eight sons — seven who pass before Samuel plus David the youngest. 1 Chronicles 2:13-15 names David as the seventh son, listing seven total. The two texts disagree by one son with no internal harmonization offered.
entries.commentary:
The numbers don't match and the disagreement is in the same canonical history. Samuel's anointing scene in 1 Samuel 16 has Jesse parade seven sons past Samuel, none get chosen, and then "there remaineth yet the youngest," David — eight total. 1 Samuel 17:12 backs this up: "he had eight sons." Then the Chronicler in 1 Chronicles 2:13-15 names them by birth order — Eliab, Abinadab, Shimea, Nethaneel, Raddai, Ozem — "David the seventh." Seven sons. One missing.

The traditional harmonization is that one son died young without offspring and so the Chronicler, who is doing genealogy not biography, omitted him. Keil and Delitzsch propose this, Gleason Archer repeats it, Eugene Merrill in his Kregel Exegetical Library Chronicles commentary defends it. The strongest version of that argument leans on the Chronicler's known habit of trimming genealogies for theological focus — he routinely compresses lists, skips generations, and ignores figures who don't serve his Davidic-cultic agenda. The targumic and rabbinic tradition went further and invented a son named Elihu to fill the slot (1 Chronicles 27:18 mentions an "Elihu, of the brethren of David" — possibly a seventh non-David brother, which would make eight, possibly a textual ghost).

Here's where the harmonization gets thin. The Chronicler is not just omitting a brother quietly — he is counting. He says "David the seventh." That is an ordinal claim, not a partial list. To make this work you have to assume the Chronicler knew of an eighth son, intentionally dropped him from the count, and then renumbered David from eighth to seventh in violation of his Samuel source. That is not omission; that is renumbering. Sara Japhet's commentary on Chronicles flags exactly this — the Chronicler routinely reshapes inherited material to fit a structural scheme, and the seven-son count is the structure, not an accident. Ralph Klein's Hermeneia volume on 1 Chronicles makes the same point: the discrepancy is best explained as the Chronicler conforming the Davidic family to a seven-son ideal, not a brother dying young.

The parsimonious read is that 1 Chronicles is a tendentious recasting of the Samuel tradition, and the numbers diverge because the Chronicler had a literary scheme to serve. The dead-brother hypothesis is post-hoc; the text gives you zero evidence of any such death, and the Chronicler himself never alludes to it. The apologetic answer requires inventing a corpse to save a count.

commentary_out.commentary:
The arithmetic clashes inside the same canonical historiography. In the anointing scene of 1 Samuel 16, Jesse parades seven sons before Samuel — none chosen — and Samuel asks whether these are all; Jesse answers, "There remaineth yet the youngest," David (16:10-11), giving eight. The figure is stated outright at 1 Samuel 17:12: Jesse "had eight sons." The Chronicler, by contrast, supplies a birth-order list — Eliab, Abinadab, Shimea, Nethanel, Raddai, Ozem — and then says "David the seventh" (1 Chronicles 2:13-15). Six named brothers plus David yields seven. One son has vanished, and the disagreement is by a single, countable head.

The traditional harmonization, as old as Keil and Delitzsch and repeated by Archer and Eugene Merrill, is that one of Jesse's sons died young and childless, so the Chronicler — composing a genealogy, not a biography — simply dropped him. The strongest form of this argument is grounded in the Chronicler's documented technique: he routinely compresses genealogies, telescopes generations, and omits figures who do not serve his Davidic-cultic program. A son who left no descendants would be genealogically invisible, and the Chronicler's interest is descent, not completeness. Rabbinic tradition pressed harder, positing a son named Elihu; the slot finds a possible anchor in 1 Chronicles 27:18, which names "Elihu, of the brethren of David" as a tribal officer over Judah — read by some as a seventh non-David brother (the Septuagint and several Hebrew witnesses there read "Eliab," the known eldest, which complicates rather than resolves the matter).

The difficulty is that the Chronicler is not silently abbreviating; he is counting. "David the seventh" is an ordinal claim, a deliberate numbering, not a partial roster that happens to stop short. To salvage the dead-brother hypothesis one must suppose the Chronicler knew of an eighth son from his Samuel source, chose to drop him, and then renumbered David from eighth to seventh — which is not omission but active recalculation against the inherited tradition. Sara Japhet's commentary flags precisely this: the Chronicler regularly reshapes received material to fit structural and numerical schemes, and a seven-son count for the house of David is plausibly such a scheme rather than an accident of pruning. Ralph Klein's Hermeneia volume reaches the same conclusion, treating the discrepancy as the Chronicler conforming the Davidic family to a tidy seven-son ideal — seven being a number of completeness — rather than evidence of a deceased brother. Gary Knoppers notes the broader pattern of the Chronicler's genealogical artistry in 1 Chronicles 1-9, where lists are theological constructions, not registry transcripts.

There is also a textual wrinkle. The Septuagint of 1 Samuel 17:12 belongs to the very block of MT "plus" material (17:12-31) that is absent from the shorter LXX-B recension, which means the eight-son figure of 17:12 sits in disputed, possibly secondary, text. That does not rescue the harmonization — 16:10-11 independently yields eight — but it shows the Samuel tradition itself is layered, and that the round numbers in these narratives are doing literary rather than archival work.

The parsimonious reading is that 1 Chronicles is a tendentious recasting of the Samuel material and the counts diverge because each author served a different design. The dead-brother solution is purely post hoc: no text records such a death, the Chronicler never alludes to one, and the harmonization must invent a corpse to preserve a number. Verdict: genuine numerical discrepancy, best explained as the Chronicler's structural recasting rather than a brother who died young.

entries.question: When David fled to Nob, what was the priest's name?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 21:1 names Ahimelech as the priest at Nob who feeds David the showbread. Jesus in Mark 2:25-26 references the same incident and attributes it to "Abiathar the high priest." The Synoptic parallels in Matthew 12 and Luke 6 quietly drop the name.
entries.commentary:
This is the contradiction that has launched a thousand harmonization attempts because it sits in the mouth of Jesus himself. 1 Samuel 21:1 is unambiguous — David came to Nob, the priest was Ahimelech, Ahimelech gave him the showbread. Abiathar was Ahimelech's son (1 Samuel 22:20) and only became high priest after his father was butchered by Doeg at Saul's order. So at the time of the showbread incident, Abiathar was not the high priest. Mark has Jesus saying he was.

The apologetic moves here are extensive. Move one: the Greek epi Abiathar archiereos can be translated "in the passage about Abiathar the high priest" (using epi as a textual reference marker like 12:26's "in the passage about the bush"). This is the favored move of D. A. Carson in his Matthew commentary and is endorsed by Craig Blomberg. Move two: Abiathar was high priest at the time of the writing of the narrative and so Mark uses his more famous title proleptically. Move three (Archer): Ahimelech is Abiathar's father in some texts and his son in others (cf. 2 Samuel 8:17), so there may be two priests named Ahimelech and Abiathar functioning together, and Jesus is right.

The textual data is brutal on these defenses. Matthew 12:3-4 and Luke 6:3-4 both repeat the Mark story and both drop the name Abiathar entirely. The Synoptic-redaction inference is obvious: Matthew and Luke noticed the error and silently fixed it. Bart Ehrman in Jesus, Interrupted explicitly walks through this case, as does Joel Marcus in the Anchor Bible Mark commentary. Marcus rejects the "in the passage about" reading because epi with a genitive proper name in this construction in Mark almost universally means "during the time of" or "in the lifetime of" — Marcus cites Mark 12:26 itself, where epi tou batou ("in the passage about the bush") uses a different construction with a definite article that 2:26 lacks. Move three (two priest pairs) requires assuming the narrative is genealogically chaotic precisely where Jesus speaks, which is unfalsifiable special pleading.

The most parsimonious account: Mark made a mistake, or Mark's source made a mistake, or the historical Jesus made a mistake about an Old Testament detail. Matthew and Luke noticed and silently corrected. The harmonization industry depends on a grammatical reading of epi that the Markan Greek does not naturally support, and it requires both later evangelists to have independently dropped the name without comment, which is itself evidence they saw the problem.

Have ye never read what David did ... How he went into the
			          house of God in the days of Abiathar the high priest? Mark 2:25-26

commentary_out.commentary:
This is the contradiction that has launched a thousand harmonization attempts precisely because it sits in the mouth of Jesus himself. The Hebrew narrative is unambiguous: in 1 Samuel 21:1 David comes to Nob, the resident priest is Ahimelech son of Ahitub, and Ahimelech gives him the consecrated bread (the so-called showbread, *leḥem happānîm*, "bread of the presence"). Ahimelech's son Abiathar enters the story only in 1 Samuel 22:20, after Doeg the Edomite slaughters the priests of Nob at Saul's order; Abiathar alone escapes and flees to David, and only thereafter functions as David's priest. At the time of the showbread episode, then, Abiathar was not the high priest — he was not yet a priest of any rank at David's side at all. Mark 2:26 nonetheless has Jesus locate the event "in the days of Abiathar the high priest" (*epi Abiathar archiereōs*).

The apologetic responses cluster into three moves. (1) The grammatical move: *epi* with the genitive can be read as a literary reference marker, "in the passage about Abiathar the high priest," appealing to Mark 12:26, *epi tou batou*, "in the passage about the bush." This is the line favored by D. A. Carson and endorsed by Craig Blomberg. (2) The proleptic-title move: Abiathar was the famous high priest of David's reign, so Mark designates the period by its better-known name, much as one might say "when Lincoln was a boy in Kentucky." (3) Archer's two-priests move: because 2 Samuel 8:17 reverses the names (Ahimelech son of Abiathar), there may have been overlapping father-son pairs, so a reading that keeps both texts accurate is allegedly available.

The data cuts against each. On the grammar, Joel Marcus shows that *epi* plus a genitive proper name in this construction normally means "in the time of" or "in the lifetime of" — exactly the temporal sense it carries elsewhere in Luke-Acts (Luke 3:2, *epi archiereōs Hanna kai Kaiapha*, "in the high-priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas"). The supposed parallel in Mark 12:26 is not parallel: there the construction includes the definite article (*epi tou batou*) and the object is a known textual unit ("the bush"), whereas 2:26 has an anarthrous personal name in the genitive. The proleptic-title move concedes the historical point and merely relabels the error as deliberate imprecision. Archer's two-pairs hypothesis is unfalsifiable special pleading that the narrative nowhere supports, and 2 Samuel 8:17 is itself widely regarded as a scribal corruption (see the parallel entry on Abiathar's parentage).

The most telling evidence is text-internal and text-external. Externally, the phrase *epi Abiathar archiereōs* is simply absent from a significant block of witnesses — it is omitted by Codex Bezae (D), W, and the Old Latin and Old Syriac traditions, a deletion that the editors of NA28 explain as scribes excising a known difficulty. Internally, both later Synoptics that reproduce the saying — Matthew 12:3-4 and Luke 6:3-4 — repeat the showbread argument in detail yet drop the name Abiathar entirely. On the two-source hypothesis, where Matthew and Luke used Mark, this is precisely the editorial fingerprint one expects: two independent evangelists, working from Mark, recognized the chronological problem and silently removed it. Adela Yarbro Collins, Marcus, and Bart Ehrman all read the omission as corrective redaction rather than coincidence.

The most economical account is that Mark, or Mark's pre-Markan source, or the tradition placed in Jesus' mouth, erred on an Old Testament detail; later tradents noticed and cleaned it up, in the manuscripts and in the parallel Gospels alike. The harmonization industry depends on a sense of *epi* the Markan Greek does not naturally bear and on coincidences the manuscript record better explains as deliberate fixes. Verdict: genuine error preserved in Mark and silently corrected downstream.

entries.question: Was Jesus the first to rise from the dead?
entries.summary: Acts 26:23 and 1 Corinthians 15:20 call Jesus the firstfruits of the resurrection and the first to rise from the dead. But the witch of Endor in 1 Samuel 28:11-14 raises Samuel from the dead centuries earlier, and the Hebrew Bible has Elijah and Elisha raising others (1 Kings 17, 2 Kings 4, 2 Kings 13), as does Jesus himself in the Gospels (Lazarus, Jairus's daughter, the widow of Nain's son). Jesus is not chronologically first.
entries.commentary:
Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:20 calls Christ "the firstfruits of them that slept," and Acts 26:23 has Paul before Festus claiming Christ would be "the first that should rise from the dead." These are theological claims. The Hebrew Bible has the witch of Endor explicitly raising Samuel — "an old man cometh up; and he is covered with a mantle. And Saul perceived that it was Samuel" — and Samuel speaks at length to Saul before predicting Saul's death. Elijah resuscitates the widow's son in 1 Kings 17, Elisha resuscitates the Shunammite's son in 2 Kings 4, and 2 Kings 13:21 has a corpse revive on contact with Elisha's bones. In the Gospels, Jesus himself raises Lazarus, Jairus's daughter, and the Nain widow's son — all chronologically before Jesus's own resurrection.

The standard apologetic distinction is between resuscitation (returning to mortal life, eventually dying again) and resurrection (immortal eschatological body, never dying again). Paul's claim is that Jesus is the first to undergo the latter. N. T. Wright in The Resurrection of the Son of God makes this argument at length — Samuel, Lazarus, et al. were resuscitated to mortal life and died again, while Jesus rose with a glorified body that does not die. Acts 26:23's "first that should rise from the dead" is read as eschatological-resurrection-specific.

This distinction works for Paul but has a problem for the Samuel case. Samuel in 1 Samuel 28 is not resuscitated to mortal life — he's brought up from Sheol in a spectral form, speaks, and presumably returns. If the apologist wants "resuscitation vs. resurrection" to do the work, then Samuel's appearance is neither, and the verse can be discarded as not really being a "rising from the dead." But that just means the SAB has picked a weak example. The Lazarus and Jairus's-daughter examples are tighter — Jesus does explicitly raise people from the dead before his own resurrection, and those resurrections happen in the same Gospel narrative.

The Wright distinction is theologically coherent but it is post-hoc to Paul's text. Paul does not say "Christ is the first to rise with a glorified body" — he says Christ is the firstfruits. The apologist read requires reading "firstfruits" as a technical eschatological-body marker rather than a chronological one. That is plausible but it is exegesis-by-need. The simpler reading is that Paul is making a theological claim that doesn't bother to harmonize with the pre-Christian Jewish revival traditions. The Hebrew Bible writers and the synoptic gospel writers did not share Paul's framework, and the texts disagree on whose resurrection counts as the first.

commentary_out.commentary:
The verses cited do not in fact make the same kind of claim. Acts 26:23 has Paul declare before Festus that the Messiah, "by being the first to rise from the dead (*prōtos ex anastaseōs nekrōn*), would proclaim light," and 1 Corinthians 15:20 calls the risen Christ "the firstfruits (*aparchē*) of those who have fallen asleep." The objector lines these up against a string of earlier revivals: the medium at Endor brings up Samuel (1 Samuel 28:11-14); Elijah revives the widow of Zarephath's son (1 Kings 17:17-24); Elisha revives the Shunammite's son (2 Kings 4:32-37) and a corpse revives on contact with his bones (2 Kings 13:21); and in the Gospels Jesus himself raises Jairus's daughter, the widow of Nain's son, and Lazarus — all before his own resurrection.

The decisive harmonizing distinction, developed at length by N. T. Wright and standard in the technical commentaries, is between resuscitation and resurrection. The earlier figures were resuscitated: restored to ordinary mortal life, subject again to death. Lazarus walked out of the tomb to die a second time; Jairus's daughter grew up and died; the Shunammite's son lived a normal lifespan. Resurrection in the sense Paul intends is something categorically different — the entry into an imperishable, transformed, deathless body that Paul spells out in the same chapter (1 Corinthians 15:42-54, *sōma pneumatikon*, raised "in incorruption"). Christ is the first to be raised in that sense, and the agricultural metaphor *aparchē* makes the point precisely: the firstfruits are the initial installment of a harvest of the same kind, guaranteeing the rest (15:23, "Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ at his coming"). The cognate language of Colossians 1:18 and Revelation 1:5 — Christ as *prōtotokos ek tōn nekrōn*, "firstborn from the dead" — confirms that the claim is about inaugurating a new order, not about chronological priority among all revivals.

This distinction is not special pleading imported to rescue the text; it is built into Paul's own vocabulary and argument. The whole logic of 1 Corinthians 15 depends on Christ's resurrection being the unrepeatable, eschatological first of a series that the dead in Christ will share — a status none of the resuscitated figures occupy, since all of them died again. Fitzmyer reads Acts 26:23 the same way, with *prōtos* marking Christ as the pioneer of eschatological resurrection rather than the first human ever to return from death. Thiselton and Fee both stress that *aparchē* is a representative-and-guarantee term, not a stopwatch.

The Samuel example, on which this entry leans, is in fact the weakest of the lot and cuts against the objection. The apparition at Endor is not a resuscitation to bodily life at all: Samuel is summoned as a shade "coming up out of the earth" (28:13), speaks, and is not described as restored to living embodiment — he is a denizen of Sheol briefly made to appear. By any definition Samuel neither resuscitated nor resurrected; he was, at most, a necromantic manifestation. As a counterexample to "first to rise from the dead" it fails on its own terms. The genuinely tight counter-cases are Lazarus and the others raised within the Gospel narratives — but those are precisely the cases the resuscitation/resurrection distinction was designed to handle, and handles cleanly: they returned to die again, whereas the risen Christ "dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him" (Romans 6:9).

One can still observe that the Hebrew writers and the Synoptic narrators did not operate with Paul's developed two-age framework, so the harmony is a function of Christian theological systematization rather than a claim the earlier authors would have recognized. But that is a point about conceptual development, not a logical contradiction. Read in their own senses, the texts do not collide: Paul asserts Christ's chronological-and-categorical primacy in eschatological, deathless resurrection, a claim untouched by temporary revivals to mortal life. Verdict: harmonizable — the texts use 'rise from the dead' in two distinct senses, and Paul's claim concerns resurrection-to-immortality, not revival.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Paul's claim is categorical, not chronological: Christ is the firstfruits (aparchē) and 'firstborn from the dead' (Col 1:18; cf. Rev 1:5) of eschatological resurrection — transformation into a deathless, glorified body — a category distinct from the temporary resuscitations of Samuel, the widow's son, Lazarus, etc., who returned to mortal life and died again. The texts use 'rise from the dead' in different senses, so they do not assert competing chronological claims about the same event-type.

entries.question: How did Saul die?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 31:4-6 and 1 Chronicles 10:4 say Saul committed suicide by falling on his sword. 2 Samuel 1:8-10 has an Amalekite claim he killed Saul at Saul's request. 2 Samuel 21:12 says the Philistines killed Saul. 1 Chronicles 10:14 says Yahweh personally killed him. Four different causes of death across four different texts.
entries.commentary:
1 Samuel 31:4 has Saul, gravely wounded, ask his armor-bearer to finish him off. The armor-bearer refuses out of fear, so Saul falls on his own sword. The armor-bearer then falls on his own sword too. 1 Chronicles 10:4 repeats this account essentially verbatim. So far, suicide.

2 Samuel 1:8-10 then has an Amalekite show up to David after the battle, claim he found Saul leaning on his spear, and that Saul personally asked the Amalekite to kill him because Saul was sure to die anyway. The Amalekite says he killed Saul and took the crown to David. 2 Samuel 21:12 says "the Philistines had slain Saul." 1 Chronicles 10:14 wraps up the death narrative with "the LORD ... slew him."

The traditional apologetic harmonization works through each claim. Suicide is the literal physical cause (1 Samuel 31, 1 Chronicles 10:4). The Amalekite is lying in 2 Samuel 1 to curry favor with David — David executes him anyway, but his story is fabricated. The Philistines "slew Saul" in 2 Samuel 21:12 in the sense that they put him in the situation that led to suicide; the Hebrew makah can mean "struck" in a broader sense. And Yahweh "slew him" in 1 Chronicles 10:14 theologically — every death is ultimately God's doing in the Deuteronomistic-Chronistic worldview. Archer, Youngblood, and Walter Kaiser all run versions of this stacked harmonization.

The Amalekite-was-lying answer is the strongest of the apologetic moves and is genuinely defensible — David's reaction (executing the Amalekite as if for regicide) only makes sense if the Amalekite's story is taken at face value within the narrative even if the narrator implicitly doubts it. McCarter and Anderson both note this is possible. The other harmonizations work but only by allowing the verb "to kill" to do progressively more metaphorical work across the texts. The Philistines did not literally kill Saul; they were the proximate threat. Yahweh did not literally kill Saul; he is the theological cause behind the historical event. Stack enough of those reinterpretations and you can harmonize any death account — but only by treating the texts as if they were all answering different questions.

The critical reading is that these are independent traditions about Saul's death, each making a different theological point. The Deuteronomist in 1 Samuel 31 wants Saul as the tragic suicide. The court history in 2 Samuel 1 wants the David-clears-his-conscience-of-Saul's-blood story, which requires a non-David killer. The Chronicler wants Saul's death as divine judgment for covenant breach. Each tradition foregrounds a different cause. They don't synthesize into one historical account — they reflect different theological agendas applied to a shared event. The apologetic synthesis works on paper but it requires four different definitions of "killed" to function.

commentary_out.commentary:
Four texts give four causes for Saul's death. 1 Samuel 31:4 has Saul, gravely wounded by Philistine archers, ask his armor-bearer to run him through to avoid capture and abuse; the armor-bearer refuses, and Saul falls on his own sword — suicide. 1 Chronicles 10:4 reproduces this account essentially verbatim, the Chronicler drawing directly on the Samuel text. 2 Samuel 1:8-10 has an Amalekite arrive at David's camp claiming he found Saul leaning on his spear, that Saul begged him to administer the death-blow, and that he obliged and carried off the crown and bracelet. 2 Samuel 21:12 reports flatly that "the Philistines had slain Saul." 1 Chronicles 10:14 caps the death-notice theologically: "the LORD ... slew him, and turned the kingdom unto David."

The traditional harmonization processes each in turn. Suicide is the literal physical cause (1 Samuel 31; 1 Chronicles 10:4). The Amalekite is lying in 2 Samuel 1 to ingratiate himself with David, expecting a reward for dispatching David's rival — instead David executes him as a self-confessed regicide. The Philistines "slew Saul" in the sense that they inflicted the mortal wounds and created the situation; the Hebrew of 21:12 uses nakah, "struck/smote," which has a broad semantic range. And Yahweh "slew him" in 10:14 in the theological sense that every event is ultimately divine providence, here divine judgment for Saul's covenant breach. Archer, Youngblood, and Walter Kaiser all run this stacked harmonization.

The Amalekite-was-lying move is the strongest, and it is genuinely defensible. The narrator of 2 Samuel 1 plausibly intends the reader to see through the Amalekite: his story conflicts with the account just given in 1 Samuel 31, and David's response makes narrative sense only if the man is taken at his self-incriminating word, true or not. McCarter and Anderson both grant this reading. The Hebrew supports it too: 1 Samuel 31:4-5 uses forms of mut ("die") in a sequence that leaves no room for a third party finishing Saul off. So the suicide and the Amalekite accounts can be reconciled as fact versus fabrication.

The other two claims harmonize only by letting the verb "to kill" do progressively more metaphorical work. The Philistines did not literally kill Saul — they wounded him and he killed himself; "slew" in 21:12 is at best loose causation. Yahweh did not literally kill Saul — 10:14 is theological causation laid over a historical event. Each step is individually plausible, but stacking them means "killed" carries four different senses across the four texts: self-inflicted, third-party (alleged/false), proximate-causal, and ultimate-providential. With that much semantic flexibility one could harmonize almost any set of death reports.

The critical reading treats these as independent or redactionally-shaped traditions, each foregrounding a different cause for a different purpose. The Deuteronomistic account in 1 Samuel 31 wants Saul as the tragic suicide who falls on his sword rather than be taken. The court apology in 2 Samuel 1 needs a non-David agent of Saul's death so the narrative can clear David of the king's blood while still letting Saul die — and the Amalekite, conveniently a member of the cursed nation, serves perfectly (Halpern and McKenzie read the whole David narrative as an extended exoneration of a man suspiciously well-served by the deaths of his rivals). The Chronicler, working with Samuel as a source, reshapes the death into explicit divine retribution for consulting the medium of Endor and disobedience. They do not synthesize into a single forensic account; they reflect different theological agendas applied to a shared event. Verdict: partially harmonizable — suicide and the lying Amalekite genuinely cohere, but the Philistine and divine "killings" reconcile only by equivocating on the verb, and the spread of accounts is best explained as distinct traditions.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The suicide (1 Sam 31 / 1 Chr 10:4) and the Amalekite's claim (2 Sam 1) cohere if the Amalekite is a self-serving liar — a reading the narrative supports, since his account contradicts ch. 31 and David executes him on his own testimony; the Philistine 'slaying' (2 Sam 21:12, nakah = proximate cause) and Yahweh 'slaying' him (1 Chr 10:14, providential/theological cause) reconcile only by taking 'kill' in successively looser senses, which is why the four are better explained as distinct theological traditions than as one event.

entries.question: Did Saul's family die with him?
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles 10:6 says "Saul died, and his three sons, and all his house died together." 2 Samuel 2:1-7 then has Ishbosheth — Saul's son — made king of Israel after Saul's death. 2 Samuel 21 has David later handing over seven of Saul's descendants to be hanged. The "all his house died together" claim is contradicted by surviving family members appearing throughout 2 Samuel.
entries.commentary:
1 Chronicles 10:6 is sweeping: "So Saul died, and his three sons, and all his house died together." The parallel in 1 Samuel 31:6 is narrower — "so Saul died, and his three sons, and his armourbearer, and all his men, that same day together." The Chronicler globalizes "all his men" into "all his house."

The rest of Samuel demolishes the Chronicler's globalization. Ishbosheth, Saul's son, is made king over Israel by Abner in 2 Samuel 2:8-11. He reigns two years. Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son and Saul's grandson, survives and ends up at David's table (2 Samuel 9). Rizpah, Saul's concubine, is alive in 2 Samuel 3 and 2 Samuel 21. And 2 Samuel 21:1-14 has David hand over seven of Saul's male descendants — Rizpah's two sons Armoni and Mephibosheth, plus the five sons of Saul's daughter Merab — to be hanged by the Gibeonites to end a famine. That is at minimum nine living members of Saul's house after the events of 1 Samuel 31.

The apologetic harmonization is the standard Chronicler-summary defense: the Chronicler is making a theological point about the end of Saul's dynastic legitimacy, not a literal census claim. Archer and Hill both argue "all his house" means "the rest of his fighting men with him at Gilboa" rather than every blood relative. Eugene Merrill in his Kregel Chronicles commentary takes a similar line, reading "house" as the military household rather than the family.

This reading has Hebrew lexical support — bayit ("house") can mean dynasty, family, or fighting unit depending on context. But the Chronicler's redactional move is doing more work than the apologist concedes. The Chronicler's account of Saul is a single chapter, structured to terminate Saul completely so David's kingship has no genealogical competition. Japhet, Klein, and Knoppers all argue the Chronicler deliberately compresses and exaggerates the end of Saul's house to underscore the theological discontinuity. The Chronicler knows about Ishbosheth — he just doesn't include him because Ishbosheth complicates the narrative. The contradiction is real at the surface level, but it is a deliberate Chronistic literary decision, not a factual error in the modern sense. Either way, the bare-text claim of 1 Chronicles 10:6 — that Saul's whole house died at Gilboa — is contradicted by the narrative of 2 Samuel that the Chronicler is supposedly summarizing.

commentary_out.commentary:
1 Chronicles 10:6 is sweeping: "So Saul died, and his three sons, and all his house died together." Its source, 1 Samuel 31:6, is narrower: "so Saul died, and his three sons, and his armourbearer, and all his men, that same day together." The Chronicler has replaced the Samuel text's "all his men" (kol-anashav) with "all his house" (kol-beto), globalizing a statement about Saul's troops at Gilboa into a statement about his entire household.

The rest of Samuel — the very narrative the Chronicler is abridging — contradicts the globalized version. Abner takes Ishbosheth, Saul's son, and makes him king over Israel in 2 Samuel 2:8-11; he reigns two years before being assassinated. Mephibosheth, Jonathan's lame son and Saul's grandson, survives and eats at David's table (2 Samuel 9). Rizpah, Saul's concubine, is alive in 2 Samuel 3:7 and again in 2 Samuel 21. And 2 Samuel 21:1-14 has David hand over seven male descendants of Saul to the Gibeonites for execution to end a three-year famine: Rizpah's two sons Armoni and Mephibosheth, plus the five sons of Saul's daughter (the MT reads Michal, but they are Merab's sons by Adriel — itself a textual crux). That is at minimum nine living members of Saul's house after Gilboa.

The apologetic harmonization is the Chronicler-summary defense. "All his house died together" means the household that was with Saul at the battle — his sons present at Gilboa and his fighting retinue — not every blood relative. Eugene Merrill and Andrew Hill read bayit here as the military household or the immediate fighting unit rather than the dynastic line, and Archer takes the same line. This has lexical support: Hebrew bayit is genuinely elastic, denoting a physical house, a dynasty ("the house of David"), an extended family, or a retinue, depending on context.

But the apologist's lexical move does not fully cover the Chronicler's editorial move. The point is not merely what bayit could mean but why the Chronicler changed "all his men" to "all his house" in the first place. The Chronicler compresses Saul's entire reign and death into a single chapter whose function is to terminate the house of Saul cleanly so that David's kingship has no genealogical competition; the very next material moves to David. Japhet, Klein, and Knoppers all argue the Chronicler deliberately heightens the totality of Saul's end to underscore the theological discontinuity between the rejected house and the chosen one. The Chronicler unquestionably knew the Samuel traditions about Ishbosheth and the surviving Saulides — he was working from that scroll — and chose to omit the two-year rival reign because it complicated his clean transfer of "the kingdom unto David" (10:14). On this reading the wording is not an innocent summary but a tendentious one.

So the contradiction is real at the canonical surface — 1 Chronicles 10:6 says the whole house died at Gilboa; 2 Samuel narrates a house that conspicuously did not — but it is a product of deliberate Chronistic theology rather than a naive factual blunder. The apologetic harmonization survives only by reading bayit as "battle retinue," which is possible lexically but runs against the Chronicler's evident purpose in making the statement total. Verdict: genuine surface contradiction arising from intentional Chronistic compression; the lexical harmonization is available but reads against the grain of the redaction.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Hebrew bayit ('house') can denote a battle retinue rather than the whole bloodline, so 'all his house died together' (1 Chr 10:6) can be read as 'all his men present at Gilboa' (matching the source text 1 Sam 31:6, 'all his men'), leaving the later surviving Saulides untouched; this lexical resolution is genuinely available but cuts against the Chronicler's evident purpose of presenting Saul's house as wholly terminated, so the surface tension reflects deliberate theological compression rather than mere idiom.

entries.question: Where did God kill Uzza?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 6:6 locates Uzzah's death at "Nachon's threshingfloor." 1 Chronicles 13:9 locates the same event at "the threshingfloor of Chidon." Both texts describe the identical incident — Uzzah steadying the ark, the oxen stumbling, God striking him dead — but they name the location differently.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the most transparent Samuel-Chronicles divergences in the text. Same scene, same actor, same outcome, two different threshing-floor names. The Septuagint of 2 Samuel 6:6 reads Nodab/Nodan, and the textual apparatus shows scribes were already struggling with this name in antiquity. The Hebrew of Samuel has Nachon (nakon, which can also be read as a participle meaning "prepared"); Chronicles has Chidon (kidon, which can mean "javelin" or "destruction"). Either both are corrupted forms of a lost original, or the Chronicler is working from a different tradition entirely.

The standard apologetic move is to claim the threshing-floor had two names — owned by Nachon, sometimes called Chidon — or that one is a personal name and the other is a place-feature. Keil and Delitzsch made exactly this move in the nineteenth century. The problem is that nothing in either text supports this. Neither narrator hints at a dual name. The text in Samuel says "Nachon's threshingfloor." The text in Chronicles says "the threshingfloor of Chidon." The harmonizer is inventing a tradition neither author preserved to rescue a contradiction neither author noticed.

The critical reading is simpler. The Chronicler is working from Samuel as a base text but had access to variant traditions, or he is correcting what he found in his Vorlage. The textual history of Samuel is notoriously messy — the Qumran fragments (4QSam-a) show that the MT of Samuel has suffered significant corruption, and McCarter's Anchor Bible volume documents dozens of cases where Chronicles preserves an older or different reading. This is a name-variant, not a divinely-coordinated travel itinerary.

Nothing theologically heavy rides on the location. But "Where did this happen?" is exactly the kind of question two reliable witnesses should agree on, and these two don't.

commentary_out.commentary:
Two parallel accounts of the ark's transport name the place of Uzzah's death differently. 2 Samuel 6:6 sets it at "Nachon's threshingfloor"; 1 Chronicles 13:9 sets the identical incident — Uzzah steadying the ark, the oxen stumbling, the divine stroke — at "the threshingfloor of Chidon." Everything else in the scene corresponds, which isolates the place-name as the single point of divergence.

The original-language data is the heart of the matter. The Hebrew of Samuel reads goren nakon; the consonants nkwn can be vocalized as a proper name (Nachon) or read as the niphal participle nakon, "prepared/established" — possibly a descriptive phrase rather than a name. Chronicles reads goren kidon; kidon elsewhere means "javelin" (as in Goliath's weapon, 1 Sam 17:6, 45) and could carry overtones of "destruction." The versional witnesses confirm that the name was unstable in antiquity: the Septuagint of 2 Samuel 6:6 has Nachor/Nodab-type forms, and manuscripts of the Greek and the Syriac diverge among themselves. The simplest inference is that one or both names are corruptions of a single lost original, the consonants having shifted in transmission.

This fits the broader textual picture of Samuel. The Qumran scroll 4QSam-a, though damaged at this point, repeatedly shows that the Masoretic text of Samuel has suffered significant corruption and that Chronicles and the Old Greek frequently preserve readings closer to a different, sometimes older, Hebrew Vorlage. McCarter's Anchor Bible volume catalogues dozens of such cases. On this view the Chronicler did not invent Chidon; he found a divergent name in his source or reproduced a variant tradition, and the two canonical texts now preserve two stages or branches of a damaged transmission.

The classic harmonization, advanced by Keil and Delitzsch in the nineteenth century, proposes that the threshing-floor bore two names — owned by a man named Nachon but also known as Chidon — or that one term is the owner's personal name and the other a local designation. As a logical possibility this cannot be excluded: ancient sites did sometimes carry alternate names (compare Bethel/Luz, Jebus/Jerusalem). The steel-manned version of the argument notes that dual toponyms are well attested, so a single floor with two designations is not implausible in principle.

The weakness is evidentiary, not logical. Neither narrator gives any hint of a second name — no "which is also called," no apposition, no gloss of the kind the biblical writers regularly supply when they do equate two place-names. Samuel simply says Nachon; Chronicles simply says Chidon. The dual-name solution must therefore postulate a tradition that neither text preserves in order to reconcile a difference that, on the manuscript evidence, looks like ordinary scribal divergence in a notoriously unstable book. The harmonization is possible but unmotivated; the corruption hypothesis is both motivated and economical.

Nothing of theological weight rides on the location — no doctrine depends on whether the floor was Nachon's or Chidon's. But the question is precisely the kind of mundane factual detail on which two faithful witnesses to the same event would be expected to agree, and the Hebrew Bible's two reports do not. The honest conclusion is that this is a name-variant generated in transmission rather than a coordinated record.

Verdict: textual corruption / divergent tradition — most plausibly a single original name garbled in the transmission of an unstable Samuel text, not a contradiction either author intended.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The divergence is most economically explained as a transmissional name-variant: the Hebrew consonants nkwn (Nachon) and kydn (Chidon), unstable across LXX and Syriac witnesses and consistent with the well-documented corruption of MT Samuel (4QSam-a), point to a single lost original rather than two different events; the dual-name proposal is also logically possible but textually unsupported.

entries.question: When did Absalom rebel against David?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 15:7 reports Absalom's rebellion begins "after forty years." 2 Samuel 5:4 states David reigned only forty years total. If 15:7 is read as forty years into David's reign, the rebellion comes at the very end of his life — but the rebellion narrative is followed by years of additional reign and the eventual succession of Solomon, which is internally inconsistent.
entries.commentary:
This one is an internal Samuel problem, not a Samuel-versus-Chronicles problem. 2 Samuel 5:4 sets David's total reign at 40 years. 2 Samuel 15:7 then says "after forty years" Absalom hatched his Hebron coup. If "forty years" counts from the start of David's reign, then Absalom rebelled in the last year, which leaves no room for everything 2 Samuel 16-24 and 1 Kings 1-2 describes happening afterward — David's flight, the Mahanaim period, the return, the Sheba revolt, the census, the threshing-floor purchase, the succession struggle.

The Septuagint and the Syriac Peshitta and a few Hebrew manuscripts read "after four years" rather than "after forty" at 2 Samuel 15:7. Most critical scholars, including McCarter in the Anchor Bible volume, take "four" as the original reading and "forty" as a textual corruption — probably a scribe assimilating to the round number forty that appears so often in Samuel. Even Josephus, in Antiquities 7.196, knows the tradition as "four years."

So the apologetic move here is actually the same as the critical one: the MT "forty" is a textual error and the original was "four." Where critic and apologist part ways is what to do with that admission. The critic says: this is normal for ancient texts, MT Samuel is full of these corruptions, the Bible is a human document. The apologist says: the autographs were inerrant, the transmission introduced errors, but the underlying text is recoverable. Either way, you can't get out of this contradiction without conceding that one of the canonical texts has an error.

There is also a harmonization that tries to read "forty years" as counting from David's anointing by Samuel rather than from the start of his Hebron reign, but the chronology still doesn't work out cleanly, and nothing in the text signals such a counting scheme.

Thackeray and Ralph Marcus (Harvard, 1934), preserving the "four years" tradition.

commentary_out.commentary:
This tension is internal to 2 Samuel rather than a Samuel-Chronicles parallel. 2 Samuel 5:4 fixes David's total reign at forty years: "David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years." 2 Samuel 15:7 then opens the account of Absalom's coup at Hebron with "after forty years." If the forty of 15:7 is reckoned from the start of David's reign, the rebellion falls in his final year — yet the narrative that follows requires substantial elapsed time: David's flight across the Jordan, the Mahanaim period, the defeat and death of Absalom, the return to Jerusalem, the revolt of Sheba (2 Sam 20), the events of the appended chapters (2 Sam 21-24), and ultimately the succession crisis and Solomon's accession in 1 Kings 1-2. A rebellion in the fortieth year leaves no room for any of it. Read straightforwardly, the two figures cannot both stand.

The textual evidence strongly suggests the figure in 15:7 is corrupt. The Septuagint (in major witnesses), the Syriac Peshitta, the Vulgate, and several Hebrew manuscripts read "after four years" rather than "forty." Josephus, in Antiquities 7.196, likewise knows the interval as four years. The most probable mechanism is scribal assimilation: forty (arbaim) is a stock round number in Samuel and the surrounding narratives — David's reign, the years of various judges and oppressions — and a copyist plausibly expanded an original "four" (arba) to the familiar "forty." Most critical commentators, including McCarter, adopt "four years" as the original reading, counted most naturally from some fixed point such as Absalom's return to Jerusalem or his reconciliation with David, both narrated shortly before in 2 Samuel 14.

On this passage the apologetic and critical analyses again converge: the standard conservative treatment also takes the MT's "forty" as a transmission error and "four" as the autographic reading. The two camps agree on the diagnosis and differ only on the inference. The critic regards the corruption as a normal, expected feature of an ancient hand-copied text and as evidence that Scripture is a human document subject to scribal accident. The confessional reader locates inerrancy in the autographs and treats the recoverable "four" as vindicating the original while conceding error in the received MT. Either way, the contradiction within the canonical Hebrew text is genuine and is resolved only by judging one reading mistaken.

A second harmonization tries to preserve the MT's "forty" by counting it not from David's accession but from his anointing by Samuel (1 Sam 16) or from some other earlier benchmark, so that forty years from the anointing might fall within his reign. The arithmetic, however, does not cohere cleanly with the ages and regnal totals the text supplies, and — decisively — nothing in 15:7 signals such an alternative epoch. The verse gives a bare "after forty years" with no antecedent to anchor the count to an anointing rather than to the reign just enumerated in chapter 5. The proposal rescues the number only by supplying a reckoning scheme the text never states, and it is generally regarded as forced even by those sympathetic to harmonization.

Verdict: scribal corruption in MT Samuel — the original almost certainly read "four years" (so LXX, Peshitta, Vulgate, Josephus); the internal contradiction is real in the received text and dissolves once the textual error is recognized.

entries.question: Who was Amasa's father?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 17:25 identifies Amasa's father as Ithra "an Israelite." 1 Chronicles 2:17 identifies him as Jether "the Ishmaelite." The discrepancy is both in the form of the name and, more importantly, in the ethnicity.
entries.commentary:
Two questions here. First, is the name Ithra or Jether? That one is easy — they are variant spellings of the same Hebrew name (yeter / yitra), and this kind of variation is normal in Hebrew transmission. Not a real contradiction at the name level.

The ethnicity is the real problem. Samuel says yisre'eli, "Israelite." Chronicles says yishme'eli, "Ishmaelite." The Hebrew words differ by a single letter and a vowel pattern, so a scribal error in one direction or the other is mechanically plausible. But which is the corruption? The Septuagint of 2 Samuel 17:25 reads "Jezreelite" (yizre'eli) in some manuscripts and "Ishmaelite" in others. McCarter and most critical commentators reconstruct the original as "Ishmaelite," matching Chronicles — partly because identifying David's nephew's father as a plain "Israelite" is uninformative (everyone in the narrative is Israelite, so calling Ithra one tells the reader nothing), and partly because Chronicles tends to preserve older readings against MT Samuel in many cases.

The harmonization is to say Ithra was an Ishmaelite by birth who resided among Israelites and adopted Israelite identity, or that the two terms designate different things — birth versus residency. That's not impossible. But it's a story neither text actually tells. Neither narrator says "He was born Ishmaelite but lived as Israelite." Each gives one designation flatly.

The simplest reading is that the Samuel text suffered a single-letter corruption from yishme'eli to yisre'eli — the kind of mistake medieval scribes made constantly — and Chronicles preserves the older reading. That makes Amasa half-Ishmaelite, which is actually theologically interesting given that he becomes David's army commander. A non-Israelite at the top of the Davidic military hierarchy is the kind of detail the Chronicler had little motivation to invent.

commentary_out.commentary:
Two distinct questions are folded into this contradiction, and they are not of equal weight. The first concerns the form of the father's name: 2 Samuel 17:25 calls him Ithra (Hebrew yitra'), while 1 Chronicles 2:17 calls him Jether (yeter). These are not competing identities but variant vocalizations of the same triliteral root y-t-r, and the alternation between a fuller and a contracted form of the same name is entirely ordinary in the transmission of Hebrew proper names. The Masoretes themselves preserved such doublets without comment. At the level of the name, then, there is no genuine contradiction—only orthographic variation of a kind the textual tradition produces constantly.

The ethnic designation is the substantive problem. 2 Samuel 17:25 in the Masoretic Text calls Ithra a yisre'eli, an "Israelite," whereas 1 Chronicles 2:17 calls Jether a yishme'eli, an "Ishmaelite." The two words differ by a single consonant and a shift in vowel pattern (yiśrĕ'ēlî vs. yišmĕ'ēlî), which makes a copying error in one direction or the other mechanically plausible: the medial mem and resh, together with the surrounding letters, lie within easy reach of scribal confusion, and the loss or substitution of a single consonant is among the commonest classes of error in the Hebrew tradition. The decisive question is which reading is original.

The versional evidence points away from the Masoretic "Israelite." The Septuagint of 2 Samuel 17:25 does not read "Israelite" at all: the major witnesses read Iezraēlitēs, "Jezreelite" (yizrĕ'ē'lî), and the Lucianic and other strands reflect "Ishmaelite," agreeing with Chronicles. The Vulgate likewise has Iezrahelites. That the Greek and Latin traditions diverge from MT here, and that one significant strand converges on Chronicles, tells against the Masoretic reading being primary. McCarter and most critical commentators reconstruct the original as "Ishmaelite," matching 1 Chronicles 2:17, on two grounds: first, that calling a man simply "an Israelite" within an Israelite narrative is informationally empty—the designation does no work, whereas "Ishmaelite" identifies a meaningful ethnic origin; and second, that Chronicles, despite its later date, frequently preserves an older or superior reading of the Samuel material against the Masoretic Samuel text, a phenomenon dramatically confirmed by the Qumran Samuel scrolls (4QSam-a), which repeatedly side with the Chronicler and the Septuagint against MT.

The harmonizing options are real but weak. One proposal is that yitra'/yeter was an Ishmaelite by descent who had taken up residence among Israelites, so that one text records his birth-ethnicity and the other his adopted civic identity. This is not impossible in principle—the concept of the resident alien (gēr) is well established—but it is a story neither text tells. Neither narrator says "born an Ishmaelite, naturalized as an Israelite"; each gives a single, flat designation. A second proposal treats the two terms as describing different things, ethnicity versus geography, which only works if one emends to "Jezreelite," and that emendation is itself an admission that the MT as it stands is not original.

The most economical account is that the Samuel text suffered a one-consonant corruption from yišmĕ'ēlî to yiśrĕ'ēlî and that Chronicles preserves the older reading. This yields a genealogically interesting result: Amasa, who became commander of David's (and earlier Absalom's) army, was half-Ishmaelite, a non-Israelite at the apex of the Davidic military hierarchy. The verse also sits inside a knotty genealogical problem—2 Samuel 17:25 makes Amasa's mother Abigail the daughter of Nahash and sister of Zeruiah, while 1 Chronicles 2:16 makes Abigail and Zeruiah daughters of Jesse—so the pericope is independently known to be textually disturbed. Verdict: harmonizable as variant name-forms, but the ethnic discrepancy is best explained as a scribal corruption in MT Samuel, with Chronicles preserving the older "Ishmaelite."
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The name difference (Ithra/Jether) is a routine orthographic variant of one Hebrew name. The ethnic difference resolves not by reconciliation of two true statements but by recognizing a single-consonant scribal corruption in MT 2 Samuel 17:25 (yiśrĕ'ēlî for original yišmĕ'ēlî), with the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Chronicles witnessing against the Masoretic reading.

entries.question: How many sons did Absalom have?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 14:27 says three sons were born to Absalom. 2 Samuel 18:18 has Absalom himself saying he has no son to keep his name in remembrance, which is why he set up a memorial pillar. Both statements appear in the same book about the same person.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest internal contradictions in Samuel. Chapter 14 reports three sons by name (well, by number — only the daughter Tamar is named). Chapter 18 has Absalom explaining the existence of his memorial pillar by saying he has no son to keep his name alive. Both can't be straightforwardly true of the same man at the same time.

The traditional harmonization is that Absalom's three sons died young. Childhood mortality in the ancient Near East was brutal, the argument goes — three boys could easily have died before reaching the age where they'd carry on a father's name. The pillar in 2 Samuel 18:18 is then explained as something Absalom set up after the deaths of his sons, when he realized his name would die with him. The explicit "sons died young" reading is a rabbinic harmonization; Josephus in Antiquities 7.243 simply records Absalom's stated motivation for the pillar ("if his children should perish, his name would remain by that pillar") without asserting that the sons actually died.

The problem with that reading is that the text never says it. 2 Samuel 14:27 reports the births as a piece of straightforward biographical data, no death notice attached. 2 Samuel 18:18 doesn't say "after his sons died." The harmonization works by importing a death event neither narrator mentioned and which the chronology of Absalom's relatively short adult life makes tight to fit.

The other harmonization is that 14:27 refers to sons who would later be born — that is, Absalom's projected future progeny — but the verb is past-tense Hebrew narrative consecutive, not a prediction. The critical reading is that Samuel is composite, drawing on multiple source traditions, and the contradiction reflects the editor's failure to harmonize a notice about Absalom's family in one source with a notice about the pillar in another. The pillar in 18:18 is the older, more weight-bearing tradition — it explains a real monument the original audience would have known. The three-sons notice in 14:27 is biographical fill that doesn't connect to anything else in the narrative.
